item.title: Quantitative $T_2^*$ Fidelity in Accelerated Radial Ultrashort-Echo-Time MRI of the Lumbar Cartilage Endplate: A Synthetic Computational Validation Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.00005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The lumbar cartilage endplate (CEP) is a short-$T_2^*$ structure whose composition has been linked to disc health. Ultrashort-echo-time (UTE) MRI enables direct CEP visualization, but acceleration and reconstruction may alter quantitative $T_2^*$ even when image quality improves. We evaluated how radial undersampling and reconstruction strategy affect CEP $T_2^*$ fidelity in a fully synthetic setting. A 96 x 96 sagittal lumbar phantom with five CEP levels (ground-truth $T_2^*$: 24, 22, 20, 18, and 16 ms) was simulated with six UTE echoes, eight receive coils, and radial sampling. Acceleration factors $R=1,2,4,6,8$ used 302, 151, 76, 50, and 38 spokes, respectively. Reconstructions were CG-SENSE, joint multi-echo FISTA, and direct model-based estimation from k-space. Twenty independent complex-noise realizations were evaluated per acceleration. Direct model-map RMSE increased from 0.172 ms at $R=1$ to 0.800 ms at $R=4$, 1.472 ms at $R=6$, and 2.256 ms at $R=8$. At $R=4$, joint-FISTA had lower image NRMSE than the direct model (0.132 vs. 0.203), while the direct map had lower level-wise $T_2^*$ RMSE than CG-SENSE and joint-FISTA ROI fits (0.800 vs. 1.448 and 1.288 ms; estimators differed). At $R=8$, CG-SENSE ROI fitting had the lowest $T_2^*$ RMSE (1.501 ms), whereas the direct model showed systematic underestimation (bias, -2.136 ms; CCC, 0.723). Image fidelity and quantitative biomarker fidelity therefore diverged under radial acceleration. In this synthetic framework, $R=4$ was a promising operating point for direct CEP $T_2^*$ mapping, whereas $R=8$ produced substantial bias and spatial instability. Scanner, phantom, and in vivo validation are required before clinical translation.
item.dc:creator: Yousef Riyazifar

item.title: Neonatal EEG Seizure Prediction with Quantum Inspired Continuous-Variable (Bosonic) Reservoir Computing
item.description: arXiv:2611.00008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study short-horizon neonatal seizure prediction on Helsinki-style (HUH) preprocessed EEG feature tables using quantum-inspired reservoir computing. Under strict subject-wise cross-validation on imbalanced preictal--interictal windows, we test whether reservoir constructions shaped after (i) gate-based qubit dynamics and (ii) continuous-variable (bosonic/photonic) dynamics provide a practical sequence encoder relative to strong classical baselines. Both reservoirs are executed here purely in classical simulation on a single GPU; accordingly, we do not claim quantum advantage, but rather evaluate whether quantum-shaped dynamics act as useful, low-footprint random feature maps with a trained linear readout. We compare against Random Forests and RBF--SVMs, and report AUROC, AUPRC, per-subject AUPRC, expected calibration error, and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals. Across our experiments, the CV/bosonic reservoir is consistently competitive and can improve AUPRC over the baselines, while the gate-style reservoir is more sensitive to hyperparameters. These results suggest that quantum-inspired, photonics-motivated reservoirs can be practical sequence encoders for neonatal EEG feature tables under conservative subject-wise evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Krishna Bhatia, Chun-Yu Lin

item.title: Inhalation-exhalation asymmetry in pressure-driven airflow through a population-derived median unilateral human nasal cavity
item.description: arXiv:2611.00012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study investigates inhalation-exhalation asymmetry in population-derived median unilateral human nasal cavity under pressure-driven breathing using time-resolved computational fluid dynamics (CFD). A standardized geometry reconstructed from averaged CT data of 30 adults was subjected to a sinusoidal nasopharyngeal pressure waveform over a complete breathing cycle. Low, intermediate, and high pressure amplitudes were considered to quantify breathing-phase-dependent changes in flow rate, Reynolds number, wall shear stress, nasal resistance, and olfactory-region airflow. For identical imposed pressure magnitudes, inhalation produced a consistently larger flow rate and lower aerodynamic resistance than exhalation, demonstrating a direction-dependent pressure-flow response. Increasing breathing intensity increased Reynolds number and nasal resistance while largely preserving the spatial pattern of the flow. During inhalation, stronger airflow penetrated further into the superior nasal cavity and produced higher and more localized wall shear stress, whereas exhalation exhibited smoother airflow redistribution. The breathing-phase asymmetry also affected regional ventilation: the fraction of total airflow reaching the olfactory region increased with inspiratory intensity and reached approximately 6% under the high-pressure condition, while the expiratory fraction remained comparatively insensitive to breathing intensity. These results demonstrate that pressure-driven transient simulations naturally capture geometry-dependent inhalation-exhalation differences that are suppressed when identical flow rates are prescribed for the two breathing phases, with consequences for both global nasal resistance and regional airflow delivery.
item.dc:creator: Makesh Singh, Shashwat Bhattacharya, Gaurav Bhutani

item.title: A Computational Journey Toward an Optimal Design for Metamaterial Epicardial Passive Sleeves
item.description: arXiv:2611.00013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heart failure (HF) following myocardial infarction (MI) is a major clinical challenge with severe complications. Epicardial sleeves and patches are increasingly investigated to improve heart function post-MI, yet their passive mechanical effects remain underexplored. This has resulted in limited insight into how sleeves mechanically interact with the infarct and remote myocardium. This study used 3-D in-silico cardiac models to examine how sleeve shape, material properties, and architecture affect global and regional mechanics. A high-fidelity biventricular model is used to investigate how a continuum cardiac sleeve alters function. Designs that improve regional mechanics successfully limited pathological bulging, modulated fiber strains, and influenced torsional behavior without over-constraining remote tissue, whereas overly restrictive and stiff sleeves penalized healthy myocardium and reduced the intended relief of infarct bulging. These findings highlight the importance of considering regional biomechanical markers when developing sleeve designs. Building on these continuum sleeve insights, a spheroidal left ventricle model demonstrated the proof-of-concept advantage of an "auxetic" metamaterial sleeve, engineered with a negative Poisson ratio. This programmed architecture provided region-specific benefits beyond those of conventional continuum sleeves. Ultimately, this work contributes to an improved understanding of passive sleeve-heart interactions and improves the targeted biomechanical support therapies following MI.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Naeini, V. et al. (2026). A computational journey toward an optimal design for metamaterial epicardial sleeves, Advanced Healthcare Materials 15, e01369

item.title: DiffStent: Surrogate Adjoint Differentiation for Stent Deployment in Anisotropic Arteries
item.description: arXiv:2611.00014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present DiffStent, a differentiable finite element framework for simulating arterial deformation during in silico stent deployment, where nearly incompressible, anisotropic vessel walls undergo large deformation and frictional contact with the stent. DiffStent combines the fiber-reinforced Holzapfel-Gasser-Ogden constitutive model with an implicit discrete adjoint that differentiates the converged mechanical equilibrium without unrolling the nonlinear solver, thus reducing the memory cost by three orders of magnitude. We identify three mechanisms that can lead to inaccurate, unstable, or uninformative gradients: nonsmooth switching, state mismatch, and gradient cancellation. To address these, we apply a contact surrogate in the backward pass while retaining the original physical model in the forward pass. We show superior gradient accuracy of our method over AutoDiff and finite differencing across constitutive benchmarks, idealized stented vessels, and patient-specific calcified coronary anatomies, and use the resulting sensitivities to quantify how tissue properties and calcification patterns govern lumen expansion and arterial wall stress. Finally, we demonstrate that DiffStent enables gradient-based system identification from retrospective clinical images of atherosclerotic coronary anatomy. Together, these results establish a practical approach for differentiating through nonlinear biomechanical simulations with stiff constitutive laws and nonsmooth contact, enabling patient-specific parameter inference and optimization in computational cardiovascular mechanics.
item.dc:creator: Shoaib A. Goraya, Ajay Manicka, Aviral Jain, Karim Kadry, Samuel Ruiperez-Campillo, Elazer R. Edelman, Farhad R. Nezami

item.title: Omni-iEEG Planner: an open-source Python platform integrating multimodal neuroimaging and intracranial EEG data for epilepsy surgery research
item.description: arXiv:2611.00018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal intracranial EEG (iEEG) research for epilepsy surgery combines anatomical and functional imaging, implanted electrode locations, interictal biomarkers, and functional mapping--outputs produced by different applications and reconciled by hand before they can be viewed on the same anatomy. Omni-iEEG Planner is an open-source Python platform that brings these inputs into one patient coordinate frame for research data analysis. The workflow starts from the preoperative T1-weighted MRI, from which FreeSurfer provides the cortical surface and anatomical labels; CT, PET and diffusion MRI are then co-registered to that reference, electrode contacts are detected automatically on the postimplantation CT and reviewed by the analyst, and tractography is reconstructed within the application. Channel-indexed results computed outside the platform, such as high-frequency oscillation counts from pyHFO or time-resolved gamma responses, are projected onto the contacts and the cortical surface with their source units preserved, and interictal and functional evidence remain separate layers. We describe the design and demonstrate representative workflows on de-identified patient data. The platform is not proposed as a method for every laboratory; it is a worked example of how one research group combined multimodal integration with an AI-assisted iEEG analysis tool, pyHFO, in a single open environment that others can adapt to their own pipelines. The design will accommodate further evidence types--model-derived contact scores, virtual implantation and hypothetical resection studies, group-level analyses--as they are implemented. The software is released under the MIT license for research and educational use, not clinical decision-making.
item.dc:creator: Yuta Tanoue, Masaki Izumi, Yipeng Zhang, Chenda Duan, Tonmoy Monsoor, Christopher A. Chan, Joe X. Qiao, Noriko Salamon, Aria Fallah, Vwani Roychowdhury, Hiroki Nariai

item.title: The influence of cold wall thickness and background activity on recovery coefficients in PET and SPECT
item.description: arXiv:2611.00019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Purpose: The partial volume effect caused by limited spatial resolution consists of signal spill-out from and, in the case of background, spill-in into objects. This can be described by the recovery coefficient (RC), which can be measured in phantoms. With background activity present the RC of an object inside a phantom is influenced by its confining cold wall. This is relevant for the use of RC-values in quantitative imaging, for standard uptake values, and dosimetry. Methods: A theoretical equation for RC as a function of object-to-background concentration ratio (OBR) is formulated and combined with a correction for wall thickness. Novel analytical expressions for spheres and large objects of arbitrary size are derived for the RC of the mean (RCmean). For spheres this expression was compared to previously published experimental data exploring thick (1.5 mm) and thin (0.18 mm) walls. Results: For 10, 37 and 60 mm spheres, 1 mm wall thickness and isotropic spatially invariant Gaussian point spread function with a full width half maximum in the range 2-20 mm, the minimum-maximum values for the change in RCmean times OBR are 0.03-0.19, 0.05-0.06, 0.03-0.04, respectively. Experimental and theoretical differences in RCmean between spheres with thick and thin walls were in good agreement for 10, 15, 38 and 58 mm spheres, but not for the 20 and 30 mm spheres. Conclusion: When using phantom measurements for determining RC-values it is important to consider the cold wall thickness, otherwise significant errors can arise in the presence of background activity.
item.dc:creator: Robin de Nijs

item.title: Computational assessment of incremental pyriform aperture enlargement in plastic surgery: effect on inhaled nasal airflow
item.description: arXiv:2611.00083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background. The pyriform aperture is a critical anterior bony constriction governing nasal airflow and is clinically relevant to both functional and aesthetic nasal surgery, yet the degree of pyriform aperture enlargement (PAE) needed to capture its aerodynamic benefit is undefined. This study employs high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to quantify the aerodynamic effects of progressive PAE and identify a threshold beyond which further enlargement yields minimal benefit. Methods. A CT-derived three-dimensional nasal airway model was digitally modified to produce baseline, 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% increases in pyriform aperture cross-sectional area. Pressure-driven large-eddy simulations (LES) were performed at a fixed transnasal pressure difference of 11.25 Pa to quantify changes in inspiratory flow rate, total airway resistance, and local airflow characteristics. Results. Progressive PAE monotonically increased inspiratory flow from 15.063 to 15.252 L/min (approximately 1.25%) and reduced airway resistance from 0.6138 to 0.6028 Pa.min/L (approximately 1.80%). The aerodynamic response was strongly nonlinear, with the greatest improvement occurring between 10% and 15% enlargement. Increasing the aperture from 15% to 20% produced negligible additional improvement. Conclusions. PAE improves nasal airflow by reducing the resistance imposed by the anterior bony constriction. In the anatomical model investigated, approximately 15% area enlargement represented an efficient aerodynamic threshold, after which the dominant resistance shifted toward downstream nasal structures and further enlargement produced little additional benefit. These findings support a conservative, anatomy-dependent approach to PAE and warrant validation across a broader range of patient-specific geometries.
item.dc:creator: Prosun Roy, Mohammad Yeasin, Siena Shah, Elliott Bryner, Anil Shah, Saikat Basu

item.title: Causal Multiscale Modeling of Ocular FLASH Electroretinography: Model Development, Experimental Fitting, and Spin-Glass--Percolation Predictions
item.description: arXiv:2611.00103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Purpose: To develop a causal multiscale model of retinal electroretinography (ERG) after ocular ultrahigh-dose-rate (FLASH) and conventional-dose-rate (CONV) irradiation, evaluate the framework against published ocular ERG data, and derive prospective dose-response predictions for future validation. Methods: The retina was coarse-grained into $N=200$ functional modules. Local rate equations were formulated as Hodgkin--Huxley-inspired conductance-balance/RC reductions of retinal ion-channel and synaptic pathways. Radiation generated an injury field that altered phototransduction, a-wave and b-wave dynamics and, in the network extension, inter-module coupling and bond survival. A reduced amplitude benchmark and nested M0/M1/M2 causal models were evaluated. Results: The reduced benchmark achieved $R^2=0.9721$ and RMSE $=11.94~\mu$V. M0, M1, and M2 yielded $R^2=0.8546$, 0.8559, and 0.8560, respectively, indicating limited independent identifiability of the network terms from amplitude data alone. Under an exploratory 50\% retained-gain criterion, the reduced benchmark predicted a-wave preservation thresholds of 28.6 Gy for FLASH and 23.7 Gy for CONV, and b-wave thresholds of 29.2 Gy and 24.1 Gy, respectively, corresponding to a model-based functional dose-modifying factor (DMF) of 1.21. Conclusion: The ERG amplitude data support the causal radiation-injury-to-ERG framework, while additional observables will be needed to distinguish the predicted collective-network contributions. The model also provides quantitative dose targets for prospective studies of the FLASH retinal-preservation window and a framework for testing how local retinal injury may propagate into collective dysfunction.
item.dc:creator: Ramin Abolfath, Mohammad Rezaee

item.title: A geometry-aware framework for electromagnetic fields in GATE 10
item.description: arXiv:2611.00376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objective. An increasing number of medical-physics applications require the modelling of charged-particle transport in electromagnetic (EM) fields. We aim to provide GATE 10 users with a flexible mechanism for defining such fields in Monte Carlo simulations while preserving the native Geant4 particle-transport machinery. Approach. Our framework separates the handling of coordinates from EM field evaluation. Fields are attached to geometry volumes, defined in their local frame, and represented by analytic expressions, field maps, or arbitrary Python functions. They automatically follow the position and orientation of these volumes, including in nested and dynamic geometries. We validated the framework against native Geant4 transport and tested coordinate transformations, nested volumes, and dynamic geometry. We also compared the computational cost of the three field representations. Main results. The framework reproduced the native Geant4 trajectories exactly for all tested field types with direct Geant4 counterparts. Coordinate transformations introduced only floating-point-level differences, while simulations with dynamically changing geometry reproduced the equivalent static configurations exactly. All three representations produced equivalent transport. Mapped fields added at most 18% to the single-threaded runtime of analytic fields, while Python functions required 6.9 times as much. The compiled representations scaled with the number of threads, whereas Python functions became slower as threads were added. Significance. The framework adds flexible, geometry-aware EM field definitions to GATE 10 without modifying the underlying Geant4 transport machinery, and is part of the open-source GATE 10 codebase. It also provides a basis for extending GATE 10 with additional field representations in the future.
item.dc:creator: Marc Ballestero Rib\'o (Center for Proton Therapy, Paul Scherrer Institute, Villigen, Switzerland, Department of Physics, ETH Z\"urich, Z\"urich, Switzerland), Carla Winterhalter (Center for Proton Therapy, Paul Scherrer Institute, Villigen, Switzerland), Antony John Lomax (Department of Physics, ETH Z\"urich, Z\"urich, Switzerland), Sairos Safai (Center for Proton Therapy, Paul Scherrer Institute, Villigen, Switzerland)

item.title: Simulation analysis of a direct/indirect conversion dual-layer X-ray detector for early identification of coronary artery calcium
item.description: arXiv:2611.00519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coronary artery calcification (CAC) is a strong predictor of future cardiovascular events, and CAC burden is commonly used to stratify patient cardiovascular risk. Although CAC is typically quantified using computed tomography, routine chest radiography offers an opportunity for lower-dose, widely available opportunistic screening. Single-exposure dual-energy chest radiography using multilayer flat-panel detectors can generate low- and high-energy images without motion artifacts and provide material decomposition parameters, including calcification density. In this work, we investigate a direct/indirect dual-layer detector consisting of an amorphous selenium (a-Se) direct-conversion top layer and a cesium iodide scintillator-based indirect-conversion bottom layer for enhanced visualization of small CAC. A cascaded linear systems model (CLSM) simulated task-based detectability for a 1 mm calcification embedded in soft tissue. A complementary image-domain contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) analysis using CT-derived patient anatomy with inserted 1 mm calcifications evaluated CNR as a function of a-Se thickness and dual-energy weighting factor. The CLSM analysis revealed peak task-based detectability at an a-Se thickness of 500-550 um and a tissue-cancellation weighting factor of 1.08. Detectability remained within a few percent of this maximum across a broad range of a-Se thicknesses (300-1000 um). The image-domain CNR analysis yielded maximum CNR at 300 um a-Se and weighting factor of 0.93, with a smaller range of 200-500 um giving acceptable CNR. These results indicate that near-equal weighting of the two detector layers improves anatomical-noise suppression and CAC conspicuity, while a 300 um a-Se top layer provides a practical design compromise between detectability, operating voltage, and manufacturability.
item.dc:creator: Akyl Swaby (Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of California, Santa Cruz), Linxi Shi (Department of Radiology, Stanford University), Kaitlin Hellier (Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of California, Santa Cruz), Adam S. Wang (Department of Radiology, Stanford University), Shiva Abbaszadeh (Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of California, Santa Cruz)

item.title: From Radiotherapy Dataset to Cherenkov Dose Map: A Digital Linac Monte Carlo Simulation Pipeline
item.description: arXiv:2611.01408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: Cherenkov-based radiotherapy monitoring depends on the relationship between dose and locally generated Cherenkov photons, before optical transport and detection. Purpose: To develop a DICOM RT-driven Geant4 digital linac Monte Carlo framework that scores dose and Cherenkov creation together and to evaluate their spatial correspondence. Methods: The framework converts DICOM CT, structure, plan, and dose objects into beam-delivery states and scores energy deposition and Cherenkov photon creation on a common 2.5-mm isotropic grid in a water-equivalent phantom. Static fields, different beam qualities, and a two-arc VMAT plan were tested. Monte Carlo dose was compared with TPS RTDOSE from Acuros XB and AAA; dose-Cherenkov associations and spatial agreement were assessed at voxel, plane, and profile levels. Results: Full-volume 3D dose gamma passing rates (3%/3 mm, 10% threshold) were 97.05%-98.86% for Acuros XB-referenced field-size and beam-quality cases (97.47% with AAA) and 97.84% for VMAT. Cherenkov creation correlated strongly with dose, with voxel $r^2 \geq 0.9890$ and projection/profile $r^2 \geq 0.9942$ in all cases. Dose-Cherenkov 3D gamma passing rates were 97.97%-99.16% for $10\times10$ 6X, 10X, and 15X fields and 96.59% for VMAT, but fell to 71.22% for $5\times5$ fields and 32.82% for 6FFF. Deviations were most apparent near small-field edges and along depth for 6FFF. Conclusions: In a homogeneous water phantom, local Cherenkov creation broadly tracks local dose but shows systematic differences at beam edges and with FFF beam quality. This framework supports future studies of optical transport and surface-based Cherenkov dosimetry.
item.dc:creator: Xianghuan He, Changyu Sun, Andy N. Wiles, Yao Hao, Gregory B. Biedermann, Brian W. Pogue, Rongxiao Zhang

item.title: Replayable Monte Carlo MRI: From Persistent Tissue Microphysics to Queryable Virtual Phantoms
item.description: arXiv:2611.01758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiphysics Monte Carlo simulation is the reference method for diffusion MRI in idealized tissue: walkers diffuse through a numerical substrate with relaxation, permeability, susceptibility and magnetization transfer, and accumulate the signal of a prescribed acquisition. Yet walker histories are massive, petabytes for a tractography-scale phantom, so current simulators treat them as transient. They are regenerated for every new acquisition, field strength or relaxation rate, although identical for all of them. I propose to keep these histories instead as a replay pack, compressed into persistent, shareable tissue microphysics, so that any such query is a cheap inner product against the pack. By storing each path as a Brownian bridge cut to the band a scanner class can play, transform coding its coefficients and contracting them into time segments, a replay pack is up to 5000 times smaller than the histories it keeps, while staying within the Monte-Carlo floor for every waveform of that class. It matches analytical solutions in pores, and MC/DC and MCMRSimulator on realistic axon meshes. At the scale of the field's largest benchmark, I re-simulate DiSCo, the billion-walker Monte Carlo tractography phantom, as a multiphysics replay phantom. It reproduces the published protocol's signal to one percent, and any waveform, relaxation or susceptibility up to 100 ms is a query of the same replay pack. I release every replay pack of this paper on the SubstrateCommons Hugging Face Hub and deploy replayable DiSCo as a public Hugging Face Space (https://huggingface.co/spaces/rfick/disco-replay), where anyone can choose an acquisition type (PGSE, OGSE, PGSTE or tensor encoding) and the tissue's parameters, and within two minutes receive their multiphysics Monte Carlo diffusion-weighted image volumes. With replay, a Monte Carlo simulation becomes an instrument anyone can query, at scale.
item.dc:creator: Rutger H. J. Fick

item.title: Detecting Muons with a Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra
item.description: arXiv:2611.01845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atmospheric muons are routinely detected with a variety of instruments, from cloud chambers to scintillation detectors. In this study, we demonstrate that atmospheric muons can also be detected with a clinical long axial field-of-view positron emission tomograph (PET). We performed a blank scan without any radioactive source, using a prototype feature that records all single crystal interactions. The energy a muon deposits in the PET crystals far exceeds the upper limit of the recorded energy range, which means muons cannot be identified through energy discrimination. Instead, we used the scanner's time-of-flight capabilities to select crossing events, i.e. pairs of high-energy single crystal events across the PET gantry whose spatial and temporal separation is consistent with a downward-going ultrarelativistic particle. Random pairings, however, cannot be rejected on an event-by-event basis. We therefore established the muon origin of the crossing events through their characteristic angular distribution. In order to account for geometry and event selection bias, we compare the measured crossing events to a Monte Carlo simulation of muons following the expected angular distribution. This confirms that the measured crossing events in the PET scanner are consistent with atmospheric muons.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Mercolli, William M. Steinberger

item.title: Implementation Science Driven Identification of Barriers to AI Diagnostic Decision Support: A Stakeholder-Informed Concept Mapping Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.02554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The clinical translation of artificial intelligence (AI) is a critical step toward precision medicine. The implementation study presented here focuses specifically on barriers to AI adoption in the diagnostic medicine workflow. Successful clinical adoption of AI requires more than technical performance; it depends on addressing real-world organizational, ethical, infrastructural, and workflow-related barriers that may prevent promising systems from moving beyond research settings. To examine these barriers, we used structured concept mapping (CM) to operationalize stakeholder engagement and to integrate a knowledge translation (iKT) approach within the Knowledge-to-Action (KTA) framework. Stakeholders co-generated 96 statements describing barriers to AI implementation and organized them into 11 clusters, including infrastructure limitations, ethical and legal concerns, workflow integration challenges, and distrust in algorithmic reasoning. These findings provide actionable knowledge for supporting AI implementation in the diagnostic chain. We additionally position digital twins (DT) as a related, forward-looking context, as they are increasingly discussed as future extensions of AI-enabled care. As such, our findings offer preliminary insights for future DT deployment, as many DT systems are expected to rely on AI-driven prediction, multimodal data integration, and iterative model refinement. Addressing the identified barriers early may help AI-based clinical tools, and eventually DT-enabled applications, progress from prototypes toward evidence-based standards of care.
item.dc:creator: Ali Fathi Jouzdani, Arman Gorji, Mohammad Zahedi, Morteza Alizadeh, Babak Saboury, Arman Rahmim, Mohammad R. Salmanpour, Ahmad Fayaz-Bakhsh

item.title: PET Attenuation Map Generation for Brain Imaging from Virtual Non-Contrast and Virtual Non-Iodine Images Obtained with Photon Counting CT Scanners
item.description: arXiv:2611.03425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study presents a transformation scheme for converting measured Hounsfield units (HUs) into linear attenuation coefficients (LACs) for 511 keV gamma photons in iodine contrast-enhanced angiographic CT images. The method is based on spectral CT data acquired from tissue-equivalent inserts of the Sun Nuclear electron density phantom. The resulting transformation will be used to develop an attenuation map template for our in-house developed BrainPET 7T system. Three approaches were used to obtain the attenuation maps. The first approach is based on angiographic spectral CT scans with iodinated contrast agent administration, and the computation of virtual non contrast (VNC) and virtual non-iodine (VNI) images. In this case, two images are combined: bone regions are segmented from the VNI images, and the corresponding voxel values in the VNC images are replaced, yielding a single quantitative monochromatic CT image. The second approach relies exclusively on VNC images, whereas the third approach uses only VNI images. The transformation schemes from HUs to LACs were established for different tube voltages (120 kV and 140 kV) and virtual monochromatic energies (64 keV, 67 keV, 70 keV, 76 keV, 80 keV, and 100 keV), showing the HUs dependency on the energy setting of the reconstructed virtual monochromatic energies. The accuracy and precision of the proposed transformation scheme were further evaluated using previously acquired angiographic CT datasets. Spectral CT can be expected to minimize the systematic error when converting HUs to LACs for 511 keV gamma rays using virtual monochromatic images (VMIs).
item.dc:creator: Heba Alrakh, Lutz Tellmann, Omid Nikoubashman, Sadaf Shokrgozar, Claudia Regio Brambilla, Ahlam Said Mohamad Issa, Keith George Ciantar, Sebastian Faby, Ali Abu arra, Martin Wiesmann, Charlotte Weyland, N. Jon Shah, Christoph Lerche

item.title: OpenULF: A Modular Toolkit Enables Data-Driven Ultra-Low-Field MRI with both Classical and Quantum Sensors
item.description: arXiv:2611.01511v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ultra-low-field (ULF) Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) offers a portable, low-cost alternative to conventional scanners by operating at field strengths below 10 mT. At these fields, two sensor technologies compete: quantum SQUID (Superconducting Quantum Interference Device) sensors, which provide high sensitivity but require cryogenic cooling, and classical induction coils, which are inexpensive and room-temperature but produce weaker signals. With conventional physics-based imaging, both suffer from low signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). Data-driven reconstruction has overcome similar limits in related inverse problems, but its use for ULF-MRI has been hindered by a lack of open datasets, benchmarks, and flexible simulators. To close this gap, we present OpenULF, a modular, open-source simulation toolkit that generates paired training data and supports end-to-end machine-learning (ML) reconstruction. OpenULF integrates a Bloch-equation-validated physics simulator, calibrated SQUID and coil receiver models, reconstruction ML networks, and an automated design-space exploration engine. Architecturally, a receiver abstract base class, a typed HDF5 contract that decouples physics from learning, and a resumable sweep engine make sensors, models, and datasets independently substitutable. Using OpenULF, we train 774 models across four anatomical datasets and conduct three design-space explorations. The effectiveness of ML reconstruction depends strongly on the dataset and the sensor. We identify a SQUID-to-coil crossover near 450 $\mu$T and demonstrate that sensor hardware and ML model capacity can be traded off during system design. Sensor and reconstruction choices must therefore be co-designed: the best sensor is set by the dataset and field strength, not by SNR.
item.dc:creator: Hanhan Wu, Yuchen Yuan, Weiwen Jiang

item.title: Detection Instead of Inversion: T1-T2 Microstructure Quantification With Detection Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2611.01790v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: T1-T2 correlation MRI has strong potential to quantify microstructural compartments without imposing a biological model. Traditionally, full T1-T2 spectra per voxel are reconstructed with an ill-conditioned and time-consuming Inverse Laplace Transform. We propose to view this challenge as an object detection task: A Detection Transformer (DETR) takes 64 TI/TE signals and directly predicts a set of compartments specified by T1, T2, and signal fraction. We achieve a mean average precision mAP@10 of 76.8% on simulated data, outperforming both our previous model design (53.8%) and regularized NNLS (66.1%). We show that our DETR approach outperforms NNLS in almost every setting across compartment count, compartmental signal fraction, and SNR. Reconstruction is orders of magnitude faster than NNLS. The results are fully reproducible from our public code: github.com/SebastianEndtTHI/t1t2-detr
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Endt, Fatih \"Ozkan, Marion I. Menzel

item.title: Prior-Guided Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Fast 4D MRI Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2611.01888v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Background and purpose: We propose PGPI4MR (prior-guided, physics-informed 4D MRI reconstruction), a deep learning method that leverages information from other respiratory phases or a setup scan, the first 30 s of the same scan, to improve 4D MRI reconstruction without extra scan time. Materials and methods: PGPI4MR is an unrolled network that reconstructs 16 respiratory phases from 60, 30, or 15 s of data, and single 3D volumes, each from 0.29-0.49 s of data, using a setup-scan image. The networks were trained once, on other volunteers, and were not retrained for new volunteers. We evaluated PGPI4MR on measured k-space from three datasets: free-breathing MR-linac (1.5T) and abdominal (3T) scans, and thigh scans with cuff compression (1.5T). All methods, including comparative models, received identical samples and were scored similarly. Results: In vivo, PGPI4MR had the lowest held-out error for 4D MRI at every scan time, and its 16 phases were ready a median of 7.5-13 s after the scan on the 2 GPUs tested. Coupling the 16 respiratory phases reduced the error at 60 s by 9.1% compared with reconstructing each phase alone. For sub-second MRI, the error at 0.49 s was 15.5% lower than that of the best comparison method, classical reconstruction toward the same prior, and on the faster GPU, every 0.29 s window was acquired and reconstructed within 0.5 s. Without retraining, PGPI4MR matched the best methods on the 3T abdominal scans but not on the thigh scans; after retraining on thigh data, it reduced the held-out error by 6.6% relative to the best comparison method. Conclusion: Prior information allowed PGPI4MR to reconstruct 4D and sub-second MRI more accurately than compressed sensing and a published 4D network, within seconds and without extra scan time. This could support 4D MRI for treatment planning and 3D motion monitoring during MR-guided radiotherapy.

item.title: Resampling-based batch reweighting for ComBat harmonization of MRI radiomic features in a multi-scanner glioma cohort
item.description: arXiv:2611.02156v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Radiomic features derived from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are sensitive to scanners; therefore, they require harmonization across scanners. In a radiomic feature dataset, some batches may be severely underrepresented compared to the others e.g., the Erasmus Glioma Database, which may provide harmonized features biased towards the larger batches in the dataset. We investigated whether reweighting underrepresented scanner batches before empirical-Bayes ComBat estimation improves feature harmonization and reduces residual scanner association while retaining grade-related information. In this retrospective, the Erasmus Glioma Database included 733 eligible patients acquired at a single center across nine vendor-by-field-strength configurations. Structural MRI acquired at 1 T, 1.5 T, and 3 T; four structural MRI sequences were analyzed. From four structural MRI sequences, 428 features were computed using an IBSI-compliant PyRadiomics implementation. The sample sizes of some scanner batches were very small compared to others, which may produce unequal precision and shrinkage of batch-effect estimates. We proposed a data augmentation approach to overcome the limitation of ComBat. We provided exploratory evidence, along with confirmatory Kruskal-Wallis tests with a Benjamini-Hochberg correction to assess the proposed method. Before harmonization, 392/428 features (91.6%) differed significantly across scanner batches (median eta-squared=0.463). Standard ComBat reduced this to 13/428 (3.0%), whereas batch-augmented ComBat reduced it to 8/428 (1.9%); the median residual effect size was <0.001 for both harmonized conditions. Batch augmentation appeared to be a useful strategy to improve the performance of ComBat for feature harmonization under severe batch-size imbalance.
item.dc:creator: Rifa Sajda Tasnim, Yushuf Sharke, Md Forhad Hossain, Rakibur Rahman, Enamul Hoque Bhuiyan

item.title: Peripheral prototypical contrastive loss for supervised medical image segmentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.02305v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robust segmentation of biomedical images remains challenging primarily due to ill-defined object boundaries. Although several loss functions have recently been proposed to enhance object boundary recognition, concerns remain about the susceptibility to unstable annotations resulting from boundary ambiguities. Here, we introduce the Peripheral Prototypical Contrastive (PPC) loss, which leverages prototypical contrastive learning to improve boundary recognition and enable stable training even under noisy annotation conditions. The PPC loss utilizes prototype features obtained from local regions near object boundaries, focusing specifically on ambiguous areas that have been challenging for existing approaches. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrated that the PPC loss consistently improve segmentation performance even under conditions with noisy labels. A newly proposed strategy, which adaptively determines the local region for prototype calculation, enhanced robustness and outperformed existing methods. Our findings indicate the potential of the PPC loss in facilitating scalable and reliable medical image segmentation, including the development of foundation models with imperfect annotations.

item.title: Findings-aware Language-Image Pretraining for CT Volume Interpretation
item.description: arXiv:2611.02327v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computed tomography (CT) provides diverse patient information and various clinical tasks, for which numerous deep learning models have been investigated. Recent years have seen the development of vision-language foundation models that can comprehensively extract clinical features, driven by representation learning that combines CT volumes with radiology reports. Existing approaches typically adopt Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)-based representation learning, where pairs from different cases are, in principle, treated as negative pairs such that the volume and report embeddings are pushed apart. In the biomedical imaging, however, treating different cases as negative pairs is not always appropriate, particularly when clinical similarity exists. In this study, we propose a supervised representation learning framework grounded in clinical knowledge from language foundation models, rather than the weak supervision used in CLIP. Specifically, we utilized a large language model to extract abnormal finding phrases from reports. We then explicitly constructed the target features that the image encoder should output, as the semantic representation of the extracted findings using a biomedical text embedding model. Our Findings-aware Language-Image Pre-training (FiLIP) outperformed weakly supervised approaches in multi-label zero-shot finding classification in both in-domain and external-domain evaluations, and also proved effective when fine-tuned for the downstream task of radiology report generation.
item.dc:creator: Takuro Shimaya, Junya Inoh, Masahiro Saiko

item.title: Feed-forward active magnetic shielding
item.description: arXiv:2406.14234v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Measurement of small magnetic fields requires shielding. For example, magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures small fields arising within the brain, in the presence of environmental fields several orders of magnitude larger. A common solution is passive shielding, but its cost, bulk and limited effectiveness motivate the alternative approach of active shielding, which comes in two flavours: feed-back and feed-forward. In feed-back shielding (the most common design), coils are driven from sensors that measure the corrected field. In feed-forward shielding (less common), coils are driven from sensors that measure the uncorrected field. The latter has the potential of providing better performance, but its implementation is hobbled by an inevitable coupling between coils and reference sensors. This paper describes an approach that employs a data-driven ``decoupling matrix" to suppress the coupling, enabling greater flexibility to achieve effective shielding across a wide frequency range. The method is evaluated by simulation, first using a simplified "flat world" in which the principle is clearly visualised, and then based on the more realistic geometry of a standard MEG system. Performance appears to be limited only by spatial sampling and numerical resolution. The method, which is data-driven and does not require geometric calculations, tight-tolerance fabrication, or manual calibration, is complementary with standard feed-back shielding methods. Active shielding is of particular interest in the context of a new generation of optically-pumped magnetometers (OPM), as the lower cost and reduced constraints of these new systems relative to SQUID-based systems provide an incentive to likewise reduce the cost and constraints of shielding.
item.dc:creator: Alain de Cheveign\'e

item.title: Deep learning-based self-supervised detection and localization of magnetic resonance imaging anomalies in artificial intelligence-supported radiotherapy workflows
item.description: arXiv:2605.24609v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into radiotherapy workflows, yet it remains vulnerable to out-of-distribution image data that can introduce unexpected behavior in clinical tasks. Deep learning (DL)-based anomaly detection for pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains limited and transparent evaluation for full automation is lacking. This study aimed to develop two self-supervised anomaly-detection framework variations in radiotherapy for pelvic and brain MRI.A two-stage self-supervised DL-framework was trained separately for pelvic and brain MRI utilizing three public datasets. The first stage compressed normal image data into discrete representations, and a second stage modeled the representation distribution. Anomaly-evidence was obtained by combining perceptual image differences with token-surprisal scores via negative log-likelihood estimation. Automated detection was evaluated for two anatomical cohorts: pelvis, encompassing both synthetic global anomalies and real clinical anomalies, and brain, comprising clinically annotated anomalies. Performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). For each cohort, a subset of normal images was reserved for analysis. Promising exploratory performance across evaluation cohorts was obtained. AUCs were 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.99) for synthetic pelvic anomalies, 0.95 (95% CI 0.90-1.00) for clinical pelvic anomalies, and 0.81 (95% CI 0.74-0.87) for brain anomalies. Qualitative heatmap analysis showed spatial agreement between detected anomalies and reference annotations. The framework variations showed promising anomaly detection performance across pelvic and brain MRI, supporting its potential for automated MRI quality control in radiotherapy. Heatmap-based visualization further improved interpretability by spatially localizing detected anomalies.
item.dc:creator: Mustafa Kadhim, Viktor Rogowski, Emilia Persson, Camila Gonzalez, Andr\'e Haraldsson, Sofie Ceberg, Mikael Nilsson, Malin K\"ugele, Sven B\"ack, Christian Jamtheim Gustafsson

item.title: Rethinking AI in Medical Imaging: Assumptions, Reality, and Reframing; Towards Physician-Centered Agentic Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2607.27428v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Medical imaging has served as primary proving ground for clinical AI, yet a decade of intense research has not translated into proportionate bedside impact. We argue that this gap is not primarily a product of insufficient algorithmic performance, inadequate regulation, or limited explainability. Rather, it reflects a structural misalignment, between how AI systems are designed and evaluated, and how clinical decisions are made. This work identifies 8 interconnected dimensions of this misalignment: 1) the dominance of pixel-only models in a multimodal clinical world; 2) the erosion of physician trust through opaque and inflexible systems; 3) the unfulfilled promise of foundation models in data-sparse medical domains; 4) the persistent bottleneck of non-shareable under-curated datasets; 5) the gap between validated algorithms and deployable clinical platforms; 6) the slow, unmonitored translation of evidence into routine practice; 7) the risk of AI displacing rather than extending physician judgment; and 8) the failure of prediction-centric AI to generate actionable, agentic clinical guidance. For each dimension, we reframe the problem and propose a path forward, culminating in a vision of physician-centered AI solutions with agentic reasoning that extend, rather than replace, clinical judgment.
item.dc:creator: Arman Rahmim, Nourhan Bayasi, Xiaoxiao Li, Babak Saboury, Fereshteh Yousefirizi

item.title: LesionStudio: A Patient-Informed Platform for Task-Specific Optimization of Emission Tomography Reconstruction and Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.39170v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Purpose: For task-specific PET and SPECT reconstruction optimization, we developed LesionStudio, an open-source platform incorporating patient background heterogeneity, realistic lesion morphology and texture, and lesion-background interactions beyond conventional phantoms. Methods: LesionStudio, a Python framework built on PyTomography, inserts lesions into PET/SPECT data using modality-specific forward projection and stochastic background ablation. Clinical realism was evaluated by physician review of 30 inserted lesions in eight DLBCL patients from a 1,579-lesion FDG lymphoma library. Quantification and detectability were assessed in FDG PET using spherical and patient-derived lesions varying in size, LBR, and site, reconstructed with OSEM and BSREM. Results: Inserted lesions were visually indistinguishable from true disease (AUC = 0.49). OSEM improved the patient-derived quantification limit from ~3.7 mL at iteration 4 to ~2.0 mL at iteration 10, but with increased noise and edge artifacts. Weakly regularized BSREM (beta = 5) achieved a similar ~2.0 mL limit with stability, whereas stronger regularization increased under-recovery. Detectability was contrast-dependent: no lesions were detected at LBR 2:1, whereas detectable volume ranged from 0.70 to 3.63 mL at LBR 4:1 and decreased to 0.70 mL at LBR 6:1-8:1 for both OSEM and weakly regularized BSREM. Conclusion: Reconstruction settings can shift SUV metrics and detectability enough to affect interpretation, so no single protocol suits every task. OSEM required early stopping for detection and feature stability but more iterations for mean-SUV quantification, whereas weakly regularized BSREM matched both at one setting. LesionStudio (https://github.com/qurit/LesionStudio), with our public library of realistic lesions, provides a reproducible framework for task-specific optimization across radiopharmaceuticals and scanners.
item.dc:creator: Narges Aghakhanolia, James Fowler, Ahmad Shariftabrizi, Omid Gharibi, Behnam Panahi, Sinan Akay, Arman Rahmim, Pedro L. Esquinas

item.title: Establishing the Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) for Smartphone-Derived Gait Measures in Multiple Sclerosis
item.description: arXiv:2606.28449v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Background: Digital health technologies allow for frequent, remote gait monitoring in people with multiple sclerosis (MS). However, to differentiate daily variability from actual disease progression in longitudinal data, established minimal clinically important differences (MCID) are required. Currently, there is limited literature defining these thresholds for digital gait metrics. Objective: To establish MCIDs for digital gait measures reflecting progression in MS. Methods: Digital gait measures were captured via daily, remote, smartphone-based Two-Minute Walk Tests in CONSONANCE (NCT03523858), a phase 3b study of ocrelizumab in progressive MS. Using an anchor-based approach, median changes from baseline at Week 96 on digital gait measures were computed for patients showing clinically meaningful worsening on either Timed 25-Foot Walk, Ambulation Score, Expanded Disability Status Scale, or 12-item Multiple Sclerosis Walking Scale. These changes were subsequently triangulated to derive the MCID estimates. Results: 243 patients with progressive MS (female: n=125 (51%); mean [SD] age: 49.3 [9.3]; mean [SD] EDSS: 4.8 [1.4]) had digital gait data available at baseline and Week 96. Median changes were generally consistent across anchors. Triangulated MCIDs are: Step Velocity = -0.16 m/s, Step Velocity Scaled to Walking Time = -0.18 m/s, Step Duration = 0.06 s, Step Length = -0.07 m, Total Number of Steps = -28, and Total Distance Walked = -24 m. Conclusion: These MCIDs provide a framework for interpreting meaningful gait changes and integrating digital measures into MS outcome evaluation. Beyond facilitating novel clinical trial endpoints to evaluate treatment efficacy, they enable objective, real-world monitoring to advance personalized patient care.
item.dc:creator: Mike D Rinderknecht, Bernhard Fehlmann, Dimitar Stanev, Cedric Simillion, Ernst Bos, Letizia Leocani, Agne Kazlauskaite, Gary Cutter, Helmut Butzkueven, Licinio Craveiro
